```{python}
#| label: setup
import json

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import HTML

from acme_eval.claims import claim

metrics = pd.read_csv("outputs/metrics.csv")
segments = pd.read_csv("outputs/segments.csv")
calibration = pd.read_csv("outputs/calibration.csv")
summary = json.loads(open("outputs/summary.json").read())

best = summary["best_version"]
auc = metrics[metrics["metric"] == "roc_auc"].set_index("version")["value"]
claim(best == auc.idxmax(), "The card describes the release with the highest ROC AUC.")
release = next(r for r in summary["releases"] if r["version"] == best)
scores = metrics[metrics["version"] == best].set_index("metric")
slices = segments[segments["version"] == best]
cal = calibration[calibration["version"] == best]
SMALL = 100  # fewer test contacts than this: a group's estimates are noisy


def interval(metric: str, digits: int = 3) -> str:
    """The best release's value of one metric and its 95% interval, as text."""
    row = scores.loc[metric]
    return f"{row['value']:.{digits}f} (95% interval {row['low']:.{digits}f} to {row['high']:.{digits}f})"


def percent(share: float, digits: int = 1) -> str:
    """A share between 0 and 1, as a percentage."""
    return f"{100 * share:.{digits}f}%"
```

This card follows the sections of @mitchell2019modelcards. It describes release
**`{python} best`**, the release with the highest ROC AUC in the evaluation report. Acme
Signals is a fictional company; the evaluation data are real [@moro2014bank].

## Model details {#sec-details}

- **Developer.** Acme Signals, a fictional two-person company.
- **Release.** `{python} best`, released `{python} release["month"]`.
- **Model.** `{python} release["description"]` It uses
  `{python} release["n_features"]` fields of the customer and the campaign, all known before
  the call. It does not use the call's length, `duration`, which is only known afterwards.
- **Output.** A probability that the contact subscribes to a term deposit; contacts are
  called in descending order of it.

## Intended use {#sec-use}

- **Primary use.** Ordering a bank's list of existing customers for an outbound
  term-deposit campaign, so that the call centre reaches likely subscribers sooner. People
  make and conduct every call.
- **Primary users.** A bank's marketing and call-centre teams.
- **Out of scope.** Decisions about credit, pricing or eligibility for any product; deciding
  who may be offered a product; ranking customers of a bank or country it has not been
  evaluated on; any version that uses `duration`.

## Factors {#sec-factors}

The evaluation reports results by two factors: age band
(`{python} ", ".join(slices.loc[slices["factor"] == "age_band", "segment"])` years) and
occupation (`job`, `{python} slices.loc[slices["factor"] == "job", "segment"].nunique()`
categories as recorded in the data, including `unknown`). Both are inputs to the model.

## Metrics {#sec-metrics}

The call centre calls the top `{python} percent(summary["top_share"], 0)` of the list, so
the business metric is **recall in the top `{python} percent(summary["top_share"], 0)`**: the share of all subscribers that those
calls reach. For `{python} best` it is `{python} interval("recall_top10")`, against a base
rate of `{python} percent(summary["base_rate"])`. ROC AUC, `{python} interval("roc_auc")`,
measures the whole ranking; the Brier score, `{python} interval("brier")`, measures the
probabilities. Intervals are percentiles over
`{python} f"{summary['n_bootstrap']:,}"` bootstrap resamples of the test set; they show
sampling variation in the test set only.

## Evaluation data {#sec-evaluation-data}

A stratified random `{python} percent(summary["test_size"], 0)` of the UCI Bank Marketing
table (`{python} f"{summary['test_rows']:,}"` contacts, split seed
`{python} summary["split_seed"]`), held out from training. The table records phone
campaigns of a Portuguese bank, May 2008 to November 2010 [@moro2014datadriven].

## Training data {#sec-training-data}

The other `{python} f"{summary['train_rows']:,}"` contacts of the same table. The data file
is unchanged from the source (SHA-256 `{python} summary["data_sha256"][:12]`…).

## Quantitative analyses {#sec-analyses}

```{python}
#| label: slice-setup
ages = slices[slices["factor"] == "age_band"].set_index("segment")
jobs = slices[slices["factor"] == "job"].set_index("segment")
most_called = ages["share_called"].idxmax()
least_called = ages["share_called"].idxmin()
small = slices[slices["n"] < SMALL]
claim(ages["base_rate"].idxmax() == most_called,
      "The age band called most often has the highest subscription rate.")
claim(len(small) > 0, "Some groups have fewer than SMALL test contacts.")
claim(ages["share_called"].max() > 3 * ages["share_called"].min(),
      "The ranking calls the age bands at very different rates (Ethical considerations).")
claim("unknown" in set(jobs.index), "The job categories include `unknown`.")
```

@tbl-age and @tbl-job break the metrics down by factor. The ranking calls
`{python} percent(ages.loc[most_called, "share_called"])` of contacts aged
`{python} most_called`, the band with the highest subscription rate, and
`{python} percent(ages.loc[least_called, "share_called"])` of those aged
`{python} least_called`. Groups with fewer than `{python} SMALL` test contacts
(`{python} "; ".join(f"{s}, n = {n}" for s, n in zip(small["segment"], small["n"]))`) give
noisy estimates. @fig-calibration shows that the predicted probabilities follow the observed
rates.

```{python}
#| label: slice-table
def slice_table(part: pd.DataFrame, label: str) -> HTML:
    """One factor's slice metrics, formatted for display."""
    shown = pd.DataFrame({
        label: part.index,
        "n": part["n"].map(lambda v: f"{v:,}"),
        "Subscribers": part["subscribers"].map(lambda v: f"{v:,}"),
        "Base rate": part["base_rate"].map(percent),
        "Called": part["share_called"].map(percent),
        f"Recall, top {percent(summary['top_share'], 0)}": part["recall_top10"].map(percent),
        "ROC AUC": part["roc_auc"].map(lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"),
    })
    return HTML(shown.to_html(index=False))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-age
#| tbl-cap: "Slice metrics by age band on the test contacts. Called: share of the band in the called top 10%. Recall: share of the band's subscribers who are called. ROC AUC: ranking within the band."
claim(summary["top_share"] == 0.10, "The caption says top 10%, which a caption cannot compute.")
slice_table(ages, "Age band")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-job
#| tbl-cap: "Slice metrics by job on the test contacts, defined as in the age-band table."
slice_table(jobs, "Job")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration on the test contacts: observed subscription rate against mean predicted probability in ten equal-sized bins. Points on the dashed diagonal are perfectly calibrated."
#| fig-alt: "Points joined by a line: observed rate against mean predicted probability, with a dashed diagonal. The points lie close to the diagonal; most bins have predicted probabilities below 0.25 and one bin is near 0.5."
gap = (cal["mean_predicted"] - cal["observed_rate"]).abs()
claim(gap.max() < 0.05, "The points lie close to the diagonal (alt text).")
claim((cal["mean_predicted"] < 0.25).sum() > len(cal) / 2,
      "Most bins have predicted probabilities below 0.25 (alt text).")
claim(cal["mean_predicted"].max() > 0.4, "One bin is near 0.5 (alt text).")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4))
ax.plot(cal["mean_predicted"], cal["observed_rate"], marker="o", color="#D55E00")
limit = cal[["mean_predicted", "observed_rate"]].max().max() * 1.05
ax.plot([0, limit], [0, limit], linestyle="--", color="#555555", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean predicted probability")
ax.set_ylabel("Observed subscription rate")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

## Ethical considerations {#sec-ethics}

- **Unwanted calls.** The model decides who is called first. Marketing calls take people's
  time, and a ranking concentrates them on the people it scores highest.
- **Age.** Age is an input, and age is a protected characteristic in UK law
  [@equalityact2010s4]. @sec-analyses shows that the ranking calls the age bands at very
  different rates. TODO: before any UK deployment, obtain legal review of whether and how a
  bank may use age to order marketing calls
  (<https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/15>).
- **Proxies.** Some `job` categories, such as `student` and `retired`, are related to age by
  their nature, so removing `age` alone may not remove its effect.
- **Personal data.** The table holds no names or contact details, but a deployment would
  score identifiable customers. TODO: data-protection review for the deploying bank.

## Caveats and recommendations {#sec-caveats}

- **Place and time.** The data come from one Portuguese bank in 2008 to 2010. Re-evaluate on
  the deploying bank's own recent contacts before use.
- **Random split.** The source file is ordered by date, but the test set is a random sample
  of all dates. A split by time would better show performance on future campaigns.
- **Campaign fields.** `day`, `month` and `campaign` describe the last contact of the
  campaign. A ranking made before a campaign starts would not know them; such a deployment
  needs a version without them.
- **Probabilities.** They are calibrated to this data's base rate of
  `{python} percent(summary["base_rate"])`; a campaign with a different rate needs
  recalibration.
